defaults.permitted_development: Across Dorset, for a house, the usual planning route for a driveway is easiest where the work is just hard surfacing inside the plot and run-off from any front area over 5 square metres is dealt with on site. Permission issues often arise from the access, walls or drainage details rather than the parking space alone. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Dorset, retaining or terracing works may need planning permission even where the surfacing material itself would not.
rules.depth_rules: Across Dorset, there is no extension-style depth allowance for a driveway or paved area. Front areas over 5 square metres should be permeable or drain to a porous area within the curtilage.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Dorset, driveway surfacing inside the plot and the access across the boundary are not always the same consent route. New or widened vehicle crossings usually need highway authority approval.
rules.roof_rules: Across Dorset, a driveway or paved area does not automatically authorise a roof above it. Once a car port or canopy is added, the structure needs checking under the separate rules for buildings or attached alterations.
rules.materials_rules: Across Dorset, choose the material around drainage first. For front driveway areas over 5 square metres, permeable surfacing or on-site discharge to a porous area is normally what keeps the work within the simpler route.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status makes driveway schemes more sensitive where front gardens, walls, railings or traditional paving contribute to the street scene.
restrictions.listed_building: If the proposal serves a listed building, removing walls, gates, paving or other curtilage features can trigger listed building consent as well as planning checks.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or site-specific planning condition can take away the usual driveway and front-garden permitted development route.

rules.permitted_development: For a house, the usual planning route for a driveway is easiest where the work is just hard surfacing inside the plot and run-off from any front area over 5 square metres is dealt with on site. Permission issues often arise from the access, walls or drainage details rather than the parking space alone. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: There is no simple householder height limit for paving itself. The planning question usually comes from the engineered works that support it, such as retaining walls, terracing, ramps or raised hardstanding.
rules.depth_rules: Front impermeable surfacing without suitable on-site drainage will often need planning permission.
rules.boundary_rules: The road boundary often decides the real answer. A paved area inside the site can be acceptable while the associated wall removal, widened opening or vehicle crossover is not.
rules.roof_rules: The surface itself has no roof allowance. Car ports, canopies and shelters are separate development types.
rules.materials_rules: Choose the material around drainage first. For front driveway areas over 5 square metres, permeable surfacing or on-site discharge to a porous area is normally what keeps the work within the simpler route.

restrictions.conservation_area: Driveway works in conservation areas are usually judged as much on the loss of historic frontage character as on the paving material itself.
restrictions.listed_building: Driveway works affecting a listed building, its curtilage, or historic boundary structures can need listed building consent as well as any planning or highway approval.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or site-specific planning condition can take away the usual driveway and front-garden permitted development route.
